Engines
ĕn'jĭnz
n. pl. (machines of war; siege artillery invented by cunning men, on the towers of Jerusalem and against the walls of Tyre)
Old French engin, from Latin ingenium, natural capacity or contrivance — the same root as ingenious. An engine is first a piece of cleverness and only afterwards a machine.

Biblical Definition

Uzziah armed Jerusalem with them: “And he made in Jerusalem engines, invented by cunning men, to be on the towers and upon the bulwarks, to shoot arrows and great stones withal. And his name spread far abroad; for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong” (2Ch 26:15). Every clause of that verse is approving until the last four words, and then the Chronicler turns: “But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense” (2Ch 26:16). He was struck with leprosy at the altar and dwelt in a several house until his death. Ezekiel uses the same word of the machines that would come against Tyre: “And he shall set engines of war against thy walls, and with his axes he shall break down thy towers” (Eze 26:9). The instruments Uzziah invented for defence appear in the prophets as the instruments by which cities fall. Zechariah gives the rule that governs both: “Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts” (Zec 4:6).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an engine as any mechanical instrument or complicated machine; and particularly, a military machine for throwing stones or darts, or for battering walls.

expand to see more

ENGINE, n. [Fr. engin; L. ingenium.] In a general sense, any instrument; more especially, any mechanical instrument or complicated machine.

2. A military machine; as a battering ram, or the like, used in ancient times.

He made in Jerusalem engines, invented by cunning men. 2 Chron. xxvi.

3. Any instrument to effect a purpose; means; as, an engine of mischief.

Key Scripture

2Ch 26:15 — "And he made in Jerusalem engines, invented by cunning men, to be on the towers and upon the bulwarks, to shoot arrows and great stones withal. And his name spread far abroad; for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong."

2Ch 26:16 — "But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction: for he transgressed against the LORD his God, and went into the temple of the LORD to burn incense upon the altar of incense."

Eze 26:9 — "And he shall set engines of war against thy walls, and with his axes he shall break down thy towers."

Zec 4:6 — "Then he answered and spake unto me, saying, This is the word of the LORD unto Zerubbabel, saying, Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit, saith the LORD of hosts."

Modern Corruption

Technical achievement is treated as a neutral good or as a wickedness in itself, while 2 Chronicles 26 credits the invention to God's help and then names what strength did to the man who held it.

expand to see more

Two hasty readings are available and both fail. The first treats Uzziah's engines as morally weightless — tools are tools, and only their use is good or bad. The Chronicler will not have it, because he attributes the success itself to God: he was marvellously helped, till he was strong. The skill of cunning men, the design of the machines, the spread of his name — all of it is help given. The second reading treats invention as the sin, as though ingenuity were a kind of Babel. The text does not say so. What it says is far more searching: the help was real, the strength was real, and the strength is what ruined him. But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction. The danger was not in the engines but in what the possession of them did to a man's estimate of himself.

What Uzziah did with his strength is the detail that matters, and it is a matter of worship. He went into the temple to burn incense on the altar of incense — a thing lawful only for the sons of Aaron. Eighty priests withstood him, and he was wroth with them, and while he was wroth the leprosy rose in his forehead. A king who had built a nation's defences concluded that the ordinary boundaries of God's worship did not apply to a man of his stature. That is the standing temptation of every successful builder in the church, and the regulative principle exists precisely to prevent it: what God has appointed in worship is not adjustable by achievement. Zechariah's word to Zerubbabel is the corrective given to a man who was building with far less at his disposal — not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chishshabon (H2810), an invention or contrivance, of Uzziah's engines; mechi qobollo, an engine of war, at Ezekiel 26:9; with gabahh leb, the heart lifted up.

expand to see more

Hebrew chishshabon (H2810) — a device, an invention; engines invented by cunning men; 2 Chronicles 26:15.

Hebrew chashab (H2803) — to think, to devise; the root behind the cunning men and their contrivance.

Hebrew gabahh (H1361) — to be high, to be lifted up; his heart was lifted up to his destruction; 2 Chronicles 26:16.

Hebrew maal (H4603) — to trespass, to act unfaithfully; he transgressed against the LORD his God; 2 Chronicles 26:16.

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — spirit; not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit; Zechariah 4:6.

Usage

"“Engines, invented by cunning men” — skill counted as help given."

"“He was marvellously helped, till he was strong” — the hinge of the whole reign."

"“Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit” — said to a man with nothing like Uzziah's resources."
